THE CROWD

Groups can be classified in a number of ways depending on the purpose and perspective of the group.

During mid-adolescence the crowd becomes the most important avenue of contact.� The crowd is a group of people of similar age grouping.� Members of both sexes are represented.� They have strong feeling of togetherness and a sense of community spirit among its members.� Friendships are flexible among crowd members with the length of friendship varying between people.� The leader is regarded as a model or reference person for all crowd members. The crowd is not bound by strong group pressures.


For�example, students may gather together at lunch to make stage sets for the school play, may be classified as a crowd.

The clique is a group of people with special, distinguishing features.� It is usually quite small in numbers .� A clique is usually structured around class lines; the higher the class, the more strict the entrance to the clique.� A clique is closer than a crowd.� It meets important goals for its members.� Membership in the clique gives a person status and a sense of worth.

For example, in a large school a small group of students form a close-knit group that sticks together at school and socially.

IN GROUPS AND OUT GROUPS

Normally, a person identifies with and builds strong links in their  in group .� Anyone outside this group is called the  out group . These groups are different for every person.� In some cases the boundaries of the in and out groups are strictly guarded to block the entry of new members.�

For example, students collect in a variety of groups during the noon hour.� Students move from group to another to engage in casual conversation.� They one day administration advertises a poster completion for a special prize.� Students may work in groups over the lunch hour.� At that point, in and out groups will likely become established and strictly enforced.� Each group won t want others to steal their ideas.� In groups will work together and out members will be excluded.

INCLUSIVE/EXCLUSIVE GROUPS

Inclusive and exclusive groups center on membership.� The aim of an inclusive group is to expand activities and include more people.� Small inclusive groups tend to change over time as they grow into larger groups.�

For example, many church groups are inclusive because they seek to expand their membership to include new members.

An aim of the exclusive group is to limit membership to those with special status or who meet set requirements.� They are seen as an elite group that often has ceremonies or initiation before granting full membership.� Members of exclusive groups may wear special clothing, jewelry, badges or pins to separate them from nonmembers.

For example, the Rotary club, police force or basketball team would be exclusive groups.



TASK ORIENTED/INTERACTION ORIENTED GROUPS

These groups center around the purpose of the group.

The main purpose of a task-oriented group is to perform a specific job.��For example, student s council puts on activities for students.

The main purpose of the interaction-oriented group is to make opportunities for social contacts or interaction.��For example, people decide to have drop-in volleyball and then social time once a week.

Many groups will be a combination of task and interaction-oriented.�For example, a weight-loss group will have a specific task of getting members to lose weight, and it is also a social support system for its members.
